I have always liked the hour just before the rest of the world properly wakes up. Not dawn exactly, because dawn can be theatrical, all pink and gold and birds announcing themselves as if they have been rehearsing all night. I mean the grey-blue half hour before that, when the streetlights are still on but beginning to look unnecessary, when the pavement is damp whether it has rained or not, and the houses hold their breath behind closed curtains. If you go out walking then, you feel as though you have slipped into a place that exists between one day and the next, a corridor. The bins are out. A cat crosses the road with the air of someone returning from a night shift. Someone coughs behind a window. The baker two streets away has his lights on already, and the smell that comes through the vent — yeast, warm sugar, a little burnt edge — makes the whole cold street feel briefly forgiving.

Walking is the best way I know to think without trying to think. Driving demands decisions. Sitting at a desk invites performance; you arrange your notebooks, you sharpen something, you open a document and feel watched by the blank page. But walking lets thoughts arrive sideways. The rhythm of your feet loosens things. Problems that looked like locked doors at midnight turn out, at a steady pace past front gardens and bus stops, to be merely stiff. I have solved arguments on walks by discovering I did not actually want to win them. I have mourned people properly on walks, when the grief had nowhere else to go and simply kept pace beside me for a mile or two, quieter than it was indoors. I have also had my happiest ideas while walking nowhere in particular, ideas that arrived with the modest clarity of a coin found in a coat pocket: call her, plant tomatoes, forgive that, begin again, go home by the longer road.

There is a particular pleasure in knowing a place by foot. Not the landmarks — anyone can list landmarks — but the small negotiations: which corner floods after rain, which wall gets the sun at four o'clock in February, where the blackberries come earliest, which gate squeaks, which dog will erupt into ecstatic fury behind a fence and which will only watch you with old, disappointed eyes. This kind of knowledge cannot be downloaded. It is earned slowly, season by season. A street in May, loud with blossom and the smell of cut grass, is not the same street in November when the leaves have turned to a dark paste underfoot and every window seems lit too early. To know both is to understand that a place is not a picture but a sequence. We are sequences too, though we like to pretend we are portraits. We say "I am the sort of person who..." and then life, patiently, shows us all the sorts we also are.

Libraries taught me that. A library is the only public place I know where you are not required to buy anything, explain anything, or become anything in order to stay. You can sit for hours among other people's certainties and confusions and be left alone in the best way. I loved libraries as a child because they smelled of paper and furniture polish and contained, apparently, everything. I love them now for almost the opposite reason: because wandering the shelves reminds me how much I will never read, never know, never even know enough to miss. That should be depressing, but it is not. It is a relief. The world is larger than my curiosity, and that means curiosity need never run out of work.

There is also the marginalia. Old books carry ghosts in pencil: underlinings, exclamation marks, once a furious "NO!" beside a paragraph I thought perfectly reasonable, which made me laugh aloud and reread the paragraph more suspiciously. Someone, decades before me, had argued with the same page. I felt accompanied. We tend to imagine reading as a solitary act, but it is a crowded one if you let it be. You sit with the author, with the previous readers, with the teacher who told you at fourteen that you would love this and the friend who told you at thirty that you would hate it, and with your younger self, who misunderstood a novel completely and loved it anyway for the wrong beautiful reason. Rereading is the strangest time travel. The book has not changed a word. You have changed all of yours.

I think we underestimate the lives of objects generally. Consider a chipped mug. Logically it is inferior: it threatens the lip, it harbours tea stains in the crack, it will one day fail catastrophically over a keyboard. And yet it is the one the hand reaches for. Its chip is information. It records a specific clumsiness on a specific morning, a sink, a hurry, a swear word swallowed because someone was asleep in the next room. New things are admirable but mute. Old things have begun to talk. My favourite jumper has a darn at the elbow that is not quite the same colour as the rest, and every time I notice it I think of the person who taught me to darn, sitting by a window with the needle going in and out, saying that a repair is not an attempt to pretend nothing happened. It is the opposite. It is a way of saying: this happened, and we are continuing anyway. There might be a whole philosophy in that sentence if you let it sit there long enough.

My grandmother kept a tin of buttons that was, officially, for sewing, and unofficially, a museum of vanished coats. As a child I would pour them onto the carpet and sort them by size and shininess, promoting some to currency, others to soldiers, others to jewels in a robbery I was narrating under my breath. She would tell me where they had come from without being asked. That brown one, your grandfather's overcoat. That pearl one, a blouse I wore to a dance where the band was terrible and we stayed anyway. I understood long before I could have phrased it that memory does not live primarily in grand events. It lives in buttons and recipes and the exact way someone said your name when you came in wet from the rain. The funerals we plan honour a life in speeches. The lives themselves are honoured, daily and accidentally, by the things our hands remember.

Food does this too, of course, and more rudely — it does not wait for you to be reflective, it simply hits the back of the throat and you are nine years old, twelve, twenty, standing in a kitchen that no longer exists. A particular smell of onions softening in butter can populate a room with the dead more effectively than any photograph. Photographs, I find, can lie by tidiness. They show the faces arranged. But a taste shows the afternoon unarranged. This is why cooking for someone is a more intimate act than we admit. You are not just feeding them. You are handing them your history in edible form and hoping they are gentle with it. Every family has a dish that is less a recipe than a treaty. The way the gravy is made, the argument about whether something belongs in it, the ceremonial tasting, the declaration that it is almost as good as it used to be — which everyone understands to mean that it is exactly right and that the person who used to make it is being missed at full volume.

Learning to cook taught me patience in a way that no amount of being told to be patient ever did. Bread especially is a stern and kindly teacher. You cannot bully dough. You can mix, knead, curse the cold kitchen, stare at the bowl as if it owes you money; the yeast proceeds at its own ancient tempo. Most good things seem to work like this. Friendships rise or they do not. Grief ferments. An apology forced before it is ready comes out dense and underdone. I have ruined loaves by impatience and conversations by the same method, and the resemblance is not a metaphor so much as a diagnosis. Wait. Cover the bowl. Do something else useful with your hands. Come back and be surprised by growth that happened while you were not overseeing it. There is a lesson about control in there that I have to relearn approximately every month.

The sea refuses control altogether, which may be why people go and stand in front of it when their lives become unmanageable. It is not comforting, exactly. The sea does not care, and there is a kind of honesty in that indifference which can feel more restful than sympathy. Sympathy asks you to perform your feelings in an understandable shape. The sea asks nothing. It repeats itself with endless variation, wave after wave, each one technically unique and practically the same, like days in a long illness or days in a good marriage or verses in an old song. I grew up near enough to the coast that the weather carried salt in it, and I still think the tide is the best clock ever devised because it admits that time is not only forward. Time comes back. It covers and uncovers. It returns what was lost, polished and strange: a shoe, a crab shell, the ribcage of a wreck, somebody's bright plastic spade from two summers ago.

As a child I believed the beach at low tide was a place the world had temporarily forgotten to finish. All that ribbed sand, those rock pools going about their small, ferocious business in private. A rock pool is a universe with strict borders and no mercy. Limpets like clamped-down moons. Anemones waving their fat fingers at nothing. A crab sidling into shadow with the guilty speed of a thief in a painting. I could crouch there until my legs went numb, utterly absorbed, learning the first rule of attention: that the small is not a diminished version of the large. It is its own scale, complete. Ants know this. Botanists know this. Anyone who has ever watched a baby sleeping, that monumental breathing, knows this. We keep asking life to be significant in the manner of mountains and triumphs, and it keeps offering itself in the manner of rock pools. Both are real, but only one of them can be found on an ordinary Tuesday.

Maps, I notice, have made us nervous of being lost, and I think we have surrendered something valuable there. Of course it is wonderful to be rescued from a one-way system in the rain in an unfamiliar city. Of course the blue dot has saved a thousand evenings. But there was a discipline to the older way: you had to look up. You had to read the church spire and the river and the slope of the land, you had to ask a human being, and asking meant admitting you were a stranger, which is sometimes the beginning of the only interesting conversations travel offers. The wrong turning had authority then. It could introduce you to the village with the improbable flower festival, the café where the owner decided you needed soup, the view you would never have chosen and never forgot. Efficiency, pursued without exception, is a way of ensuring that nothing unexpected can reach you. It is safe. It is also, in the long run, a little starved. A life should contain some deliberate inefficiency, the way a garden should contain a corner that has not been entirely argued into order.

That said, I am grateful not to navigate by stars. I can find perhaps four constellations, and one of those I might be inventing. And yet looking up on a clear night, away from the towns, produces in almost everyone I know the same two-stage reaction: first the gasp, then the silence. The gasp is for beauty. The silence is for scale. All those patient fires, so much of their light older than the languages we are using to praise them. Astronomy is the most humbling of the sciences because it will not flatter us even briefly. It says: you are brief, you are local, you are made of materials forged in catastrophes, and the sky you are admiring does not know your name. And somehow — this is the mystery — the response is not despair. It is elation. To be small and aware of vastness turns out to be a better condition than to be vast and aware of nothing. A candle does not need to be the sun to be glad of its own light.

The stars also put our urgencies in their place, which is one reason I think insomniacs love the night sky despite its role in their insomnia. At three in the morning every problem puts on its largest coat. Debts, emails, the thing you said in 2014 that had the wrong tone — they all queue up, huge and plausible. But step outside, even onto a cold doorstep in socks, and the queue thins. The problems do not vanish; they resume their actual size, which is handleable, usually, in daylight, with tea. I have come to believe that many of our troubles are not solved so much as resized. We cannot always change the event. We can sometimes change the room we are viewing it from. A walk resizes things. So does sleep, so does a friend's voice, so does time itself, that unglamorous healer who gets none of the credit we give to insight. Insight is photogenic. Time just shows up every day with a broom.

I wonder if this is why rituals matter more as we get older — not the grand religious kind necessarily, though those have carried millions through worse centuries than ours, but the improvised private ones. The first cup of tea made a particular way. The Friday walk. The candle lit for no one you would name if asked. Ritual is how we tell the nervous system that some things can be relied on. Children understand this instinctively and demand the same story in the same words, and woe betide the tired adult who improvises a line. The repetition is not a failure of imagination on the child's part. It is the point. In a world where teeth fall out and people move away and the dog gets old, the wolf must blow down the same houses in the same order. We do not outgrow this need. We only get embarrassed about it and call our rituals "routines" and pretend they are about productivity. Some of them are about survival, worn smooth into habit so they can pass unnoticed.

Music, too, is ritualised time, except it lets us feel things in public that we would never say in public. I have sat in a hall full of strangers all silently weeping at a cello and thought: this is among the more honest arrangements we have made as a species. No one had to explain themselves. No one produced credentials for their sorrow. The music made a room where emotion was permitted to be larger than its occasion. People apologise for crying at songs, at films, at adverts with orchestras in them, as though the feelings were a leak. I think they are closer to a well. Something in the arrangement of notes picks the lock and up comes water that was always down there — joy, usually, entangled with grief, because the two share plumbing. The songs we loved at seventeen stay loaded for life, not because they were objectively the greatest songs ever written, though at seventeen we would have fought for this claim, but because they arrived when the self was still wet cement. Everything that lands then leaves a print.

I also keep a soft spot for railway stations, which are music of another kind. A station is a machine for holding hellos and goodbyes at high concentration, and you can feel it in your chest if you stand still in the middle of one. The announcements, the pigeons patrolling for pastry, the man asleep upright with his mouth open, the girl running full tilt with a bouquet too big for running with. Stories do not so much begin in stations as pass through them visibly, pausing just long enough for you to want the rest. I like inventing the rest. That elderly woman with the immaculate coat and the carrier bag full of oranges is going to meet someone she has been angry with for eleven years; the oranges are a peace offering disguised as a shopping trip. That teenager practising indifference by the departure board is terrified and thrilled in proportions he will remember at fifty. None of this may be true. But the practice of imagining other people's interiors is not frivolous. It is, conducted regularly, a kind of moral exercise. It is harder to be careless with people after you have spent ten minutes seriously considering that they contain weather.

Weather! We talk about it so much in this country that visitors think it is a substitute for conversation, when in fact it is a philosophy we conduct in code. To remark on the rain is to say: we are both here, enduring the same sky, let us begin from shared ground. Weather is the most democratic of subjects — it falls on the banker and the busker with roughly the same disregard — and it teaches a person the rudiments of stoicism whether they want the lesson or not. You cannot argue a front into moving faster. You can dress badly for it and be educated. I have been educated many times. I own, as a result of repeated education, too many coats and a lingering suspicion of any forecast delivered with confidence more than three days ahead. Somewhere in the gap between what was predicted and what arrived is where most of life happens anyway. Plans are forecasts for people. The actual day comes in with its own pressure system: someone ill, someone kind, a delay, a piece of luck with no manners that bursts in and rearranges the furniture. The skill is not in forecasting perfectly. The skill is in keeping a spare jumper and a sense of humour by the door.

Gardens understand this, which is why gardeners tend to be either serene or magnificently obsessed and very little in between. A garden is a long argument with the future conducted in mud. You plant something whose flowering you may not be present for, and you do it anyway, which makes gardening one of the purest forms of hope available without a prescription. My own attempts are modest and frequently defeated. The slugs hold parliament in my lettuces. The mint, invited in for tea, has attempted to annex the entire border and shows no remorse. And yet every spring I am out there again with seeds in an envelope that rattles promisingly, behaving as if this year the system will be orderly. Maybe persistence in the face of mint is the whole human story in miniature. We know how it tends to go. We plant anyway. We are not, when you look at us properly, a despairing species. We are a species that buys bulbs in October darkness on the strength of an April we cannot prove is coming.

So much of what saves us is unglamorous and repeated. The friend who keeps turning up with soup. The neighbour who takes the bins in without making it a parable about community. The message that says only "thinking of you" and arrives, by some accuracy of timing, on the one afternoon it was load-bearing. I worry sometimes that we devalue these small kindnesses because they photograph badly and cannot be announced. But look at any life that has weathered serious trouble and you will find it is held together not by one grand rescue but by a hundred small holdings — lifts to appointments, spare keys cut, a hand briefly on a shoulder in a hospital corridor, somebody remembering how you take your tea during the worst week of your year and producing it without being asked, as if to say: the world is ending in several respects, but this, at least, is still known about you. Love, most days, is not a declaration. It is accurate attention, repeated.

Accurate attention might be the closest thing I have to a creed. Attend to the person actually in front of you rather than the version you filed last year. Attend to the street in the season it is in, to the book on the page it is on, to the bread in the stage it is at. Attend to your own fatigue before it becomes somebody else's problem. It sounds simple and is fiendishly difficult, because attention is finite and the world has learned to bid for it with flashing lights. Every era, I suspect, believes its distractions are uniquely fatal to the soul. The monks complained about wandering minds without a single notification to blame. We are not the first generation to feel our thoughts fraying; we are merely the first to carry the fraying around in our pockets, glowing. The remedy is probably as old as the problem. Go outside. Look at something that does not want anything from you. A tree is excellent for this. A tree is the least needy of teachers, and its curriculum — stay, grow in the direction of light, shed what is finished, endure the winter without discussing it — could profitably be adopted by most of us, myself first.

When I think about my own life, which at this point has enough decades in it to have developed weather, I find I am less interested in its highlights than in its continuity. The parties blur; the report cards are lost; whole years I once swore I would remember forever have condensed, traitorously, into a hairstyle and an address. What remains are the threads: a capacity, slowly improved, to sit with uncertainty without immediately purchasing a solution. A small company of people whose laughter I could identify in another room. A shelf of much-repaired things. Hands that know a few useful skills — how to darn, how to judge when onions are ready, how to fold a fitted sheet into something that is not triumph but will do. If there is wisdom available to ordinary living, I think it may mostly consist of this: knowing what "will do" means and meaning it kindly. Perfection is a bully with good graphic design. "Will do," said honestly, has fed more people, saved more evenings, repaired more coats and friendships than perfection ever has.

I do not know what I will be doing in ten years, and at last I find I mind this less than I used to. For a long time I treated the future as an exam I was revising for by worrying, as though anxiety were a form of preparation and could be banked. It cannot. Anxiety is just the future experienced badly in advance, twice. What can be banked — the evidence suggests — is practice: the practiced walk, the practiced apology, the practiced hope of the gardener, the tea made properly for someone in trouble. Practice does not guarantee outcomes. It guarantees a self who has rehearsed meeting outcomes, which turns out to be most of what courage is. Courage is rarely a leap in real life. It is a person in socks on a doorstep at three in the morning, looking at stars they cannot name, breathing until the problems resume their actual size, then going back inside to sleep and deal with them at their actual size in the morning.

So let the day be ordinary, is what I am saying, and let me notice it before it passes. The kettle is coming to the boil in the other room. There is a mug with a chip that my hand will find on its own. Outside, the light has finished its grey-blue hesitation and committed to morning; a bus sighs at the corner; somebody's cat is crossing the road with absolute professional confidence. I have a walk to take later past the flooding corner and the early blackberries, a page to read that a stranger once argued with in pencil, a loaf's worth of patience to relearn and a letter — an actual letter, on paper, which will be inefficient and therefore perfect — that I have been meaning to write for weeks. None of this will be announced anywhere. All of it, attended to properly, is enough. I will put on my coat, the heavier one, because forecasts are forecasts and I have been educated before. And I will go out into the weather we share, and begin from that shared ground, and see what the day, in its own pressure system, has actually brought.

But step outside, even onto a cold doorstep in socks, and the queue thins. The problems do not vanish; they resume their actual size, which is handleable, usually, in daylight, with tea. I have come to believe that many of our troubles are not solved so much as resized. We cannot always change the event. We can sometimes change the room we are viewing it from. A walk resizes things. So does sleep, so does a friend's voice, so does time itself, that unglamorous healer who gets none of the credit we give to insight. Insight is photogenic. Time just shows up every day with a broom.

I wonder if this is why rituals matter more as we get older — not the grand religious kind necessarily, though those have carried millions through worse centuries than ours, but the improvised private ones. The first cup of tea made a particular way. The Friday walk. The candle lit for no one you would name if asked. Ritual is how we tell the nervous system that some things can be relied on. Children understand this instinctively and demand the same story in the same words, and woe betide the tired adult who improvises a line. The repetition is not a failure of imagination on the child's part. It is the point. In a world where teeth fall out and people move away and the dog gets old, the wolf must blow down the same houses in the same order. We do not outgrow this need. We only get embarrassed about it and call our rituals "routines" and pretend they are about productivity. Some of them are about survival, worn smooth into habit so they can pass unnoticed.

Music, too, is ritualised time, except it lets us feel things in public that we would never say in public. I have sat in a hall full of strangers all silently weeping at a cello and thought: this is among the more honest arrangements we have made as a species. No one had to explain themselves. No one produced credentials for their sorrow. The music made a room where emotion was permitted to be larger than its occasion. People apologise for crying at songs, at films, at adverts with orchestras in them, as though the feelings were a leak. I think they are closer to a well. Something in the arrangement of notes picks the lock and up comes water that was always down there — joy, usually, entangled with grief, because the two share plumbing. The songs we loved at seventeen stay loaded for life, not because they were objectively the greatest songs ever written, though at seventeen we would have fought for this claim, but because they arrived when the self was still wet cement. Everything that lands then leaves a print.

I also keep a soft spot for railway stations, which are music of another kind. A station is a machine for holding hellos and goodbyes at high concentration, and you can feel it in your chest if you stand still in the middle of one. The announcements, the pigeons patrolling for pastry, the man asleep upright with his mouth open, the girl running full tilt with a bouquet too big for running with. Stories do not so much begin in stations as pass through them visibly, pausing just long enough for you to want the rest. I like inventing the rest. That elderly woman with the immaculate coat and the carrier bag full of oranges is going to meet someone she has been angry with for eleven years; the oranges are a peace offering disguised as a shopping trip. That teenager practising indifference by the departure board is terrified and thrilled in proportions he will remember at fifty. None of this may be true. But the practice of imagining other people's interiors is not frivolous. It is, conducted regularly, a kind of moral exercise. It is harder to be careless with people after you have spent ten minutes seriously considering that they contain weather.

Weather! We talk about it so much in this country that visitors think it is a substitute for conversation, when in fact it is a philosophy we conduct in code. To remark on the rain is to say: we are both here, enduring the same sky, let us begin from shared ground. Weather is the most democratic of subjects — it falls on the banker and the busker with roughly the same disregard — and it teaches a person the rudiments of stoicism whether they want the lesson or not. You cannot argue a front into moving faster. You can dress badly for it and be educated. I have been educated many times. I own, as a result of repeated education, too many coats and a lingering suspicion of any forecast delivered with confidence more than three days ahead. Somewhere in the gap between what was predicted and what arrived is where most of life happens anyway. Plans are forecasts for people. The actual day comes in with its own pressure system: someone ill, someone kind, a delay, a piece of luck with no manners that bursts in and rearranges the furniture. The skill is not in forecasting perfectly. The skill is in keeping a spare jumper and a sense of humour by the door.

Gardens understand this, which is why gardeners tend to be either serene or magnificently obsessed and very little in between. A garden is a long argument with the future conducted in mud. You plant something whose flowering you may not be present for, and you do it anyway, which makes gardening one of the purest forms of hope available without a prescription. My own attempts are modest and frequently defeated. The slugs hold parliament in my lettuces. The mint, invited in for tea, has attempted to annex the entire border and shows no remorse. And yet every spring I am out there again with seeds in an envelope that rattles promisingly, behaving as if this year the system will be orderly. Maybe persistence in the face of mint is the whole human story in miniature. We know how it tends to go. We plant anyway. We are not, when you look at us properly, a despairing species. We are a species that buys bulbs in October darkness on the strength of an April we cannot prove is coming.

So much of what saves us is unglamorous and repeated. The friend who keeps turning up with soup. The neighbour who takes the bins in without making it a parable about community. The message that says only "thinking of you" and arrives, by some accuracy of timing, on the one afternoon it was load-bearing. I worry sometimes that we devalue these small kindnesses because they photograph badly and cannot be announced. But look at any life that has weathered serious trouble and you will find it is held together not by one grand rescue but by a hundred small holdings — lifts to appointments, spare keys cut, a hand briefly on a shoulder in a hospital corridor, somebody remembering how you take your tea during the worst week of your year and producing it without being asked, as if to say: the world is ending in several respects, but this, at least, is still known about you. Love, most days, is not a declaration. It is accurate attention, repeated.

Accurate attention might be the closest thing I have to a creed. Attend to the person actually in front of you rather than the version you filed last year. Attend to the street in the season it is in, to the book on the page it is on, to the bread in the stage it is at. Attend to your own fatigue before it becomes somebody else's problem. It sounds simple and is fiendishly difficult, because attention is finite and the world has learned to bid for it with flashing lights. Every era, I suspect, believes its distractions are uniquely fatal to the soul. The monks complained about wandering minds without a single notification to blame. We are not the first generation to feel our thoughts fraying; we are merely the first to carry the fraying around in our pockets, glowing. The remedy is probably as old as the problem. Go outside. Look at something that does not want anything from you. A tree is excellent for this. A tree is the least needy of teachers, and its curriculum — stay, grow in the direction of light, shed what is finished, endure the winter without discussing it — could profitably be adopted by most of us, myself first.

When I think about my own life, which at this point has enough decades in it to have developed weather, I find I am less interested in its highlights than in its continuity. The parties blur; the report cards are lost; whole years I once swore I would remember forever have condensed, traitorously, into a hairstyle and an address. What remains are the threads: a capacity, slowly improved, to sit with uncertainty without immediately purchasing a solution. A small company of people whose laughter I could identify in another room. A shelf of much-repaired things. Hands that know a few useful skills — how to darn, how to judge when onions are ready, how to fold a fitted sheet into something that is not triumph but will do. If there is wisdom available to ordinary living, I think it may mostly consist of this: knowing what "will do" means and meaning it kindly. Perfection is a bully with good graphic design. "Will do," said honestly, has fed more people, saved more evenings, repaired more coats and friendships than perfection ever has.

I do not know what I will be doing in ten years, and at last I find I mind this less than I used to. For a long time I treated the future as an exam I was revising for by worrying, as though anxiety were a form of preparation and could be banked. It cannot. Anxiety is just the future experienced badly in advance, twice. What can be banked — the evidence suggests — is practice: the practiced walk, the practiced apology, the practiced hope of the gardener, the tea made properly for someone in trouble. Practice does not guarantee outcomes. It guarantees a self who has rehearsed meeting outcomes, which turns out to be most of what courage is. Courage is rarely a leap in real life. It is a person in socks on a doorstep at three in the morning, looking at stars they cannot name, breathing until the problems resume their actual size, then going back inside to sleep and deal with them at their actual size in the morning.

So let the day be ordinary, is what I am saying, and let me notice it before it passes. The kettle is coming to the boil in the other room. There is a mug with a chip that my hand will find on its own. Outside, the light has finished its grey-blue hesitation and committed to morning; a bus sighs at the corner; somebody's cat is crossing the road with absolute professional confidence. I have a walk to take later past the flooding corner and the early blackberries, a page to read that a stranger once argued with in pencil, a loaf's worth of patience to relearn and a letter — an actual letter, on paper, which will be inefficient and therefore perfect — that I have been meaning to write for weeks. None of this will be announced anywhere. All of it, attended to properly, is enough. I will put on my coat, the heavier one, because forecasts are forecasts and I have been educated before. And I will go out into the weather we share, and begin from that shared ground, and see what the day, in its own pressure system, has actually brought.
